cells.tense: You are here in the deep, and the pen is in your hand.
cells.ask: Show one person the unfinished pattern you've been carrying. Don't explain it — let them stand at the edge of it with you.
cells.core:
You can go deep into what something is made of, and you can come back. That's the thing most people can't do. You follow a pattern down past where it's practical to follow it, and when you surface you still know which way is up — not lost in there, visiting.

And you can sit with someone at that edge without either of you dissolving. That's the part worth noticing. You're not showing off what you found or handing it over as a package; you're letting someone near the depth and staying yourself while they look. What that does is quieter than it sounds. It gives the other person room to recognize something without having to become you.
cells.sheetLine: You go deep and come back, and you can do it near someone.

cells.tense: You're bracing at a future where the whole pattern will finally be written in.
cells.ask: Put down the running model tonight. Write the shortest true version — one paragraph, on paper — and leave it at that.
cells.core:
You're running the whole thing ahead of time, to a version where the pattern is complete and can be presented. It isn't complete. The rush to get it there has you announcing a finished structure over something you haven't finished understanding yet — the frame is outrunning what's inside it.

What's strange is that the compulsion feels like rigor. It isn't. It's bracing — you're preparing for the moment the thing will be clear, and that moment keeps moving because you keep moving past it. There's real understanding underneath. It's buried under a version that isn't ready to be said. You built a frame around something still taking shape, which is a way of not having to look at it.
cells.sheetLine: You're presenting the finished version of something still forming.

cells.tense: You stopped at a door of your own thinking and you're still standing there.
cells.ask: Finish one unfinished thing and say it out loud to someone — a half-pattern, a partial thought, anything you were about to drop.
cells.core:
You know how to go deep — or you did. When you go as far as you can into how a thing works, you end up somewhere most people don't go on purpose, and you recognize what's there. That's the part that's still working. The idea is fine. What you do with it is where it stops.

Now the thinking stays near the surface where it's safe, and nothing gets taken all the way down. You still recognize the patterns. You just don't follow them. So it can look like good judgment from outside. From where you are, it's more like holding your breath at the edge of a pool. The water is still there. What stopped is the step, not the water. That's the part that can move again — one unfinished thing, said out loud, badly, to one person.
cells.sheetLine: You know the deep water is there and you've stopped stepping in.

cells.tense: You're already down in the deep and describing it as if you wandered in.
cells.ask: Say out loud one pattern you've seen and been attributing to the material. Put your name on seeing it, just once, to one person.
cells.core:
You feel the pattern before it has words, and you know when a thing is true before you can say why. That's already running in you — at work, in conversation, in what you notice before anyone else does. And you talk about it like it arrived on its own, like the material told you, like anyone standing there would have gotten it.

That's the part that's off. What you call reading the room, or the text, or the data saying so — that's you recognizing something. The recognition is happening; the owning of it isn't. You keep handing the credit to the subject. Which means you get to keep being surprised by your own depth, and the one doing it stays out of the frame.
cells.sheetLine: The recognition is yours. You keep saying it came from the material.
